blocks.text: Walk through Mile 12 or Balogun Market with a bundle of naira notes and you can buy rice, cloth or a phone in seconds. Try the same trip with a goat and a sack of yams and you will spend the morning hunting for someone who both wants your goods and has what you want. That hunt is the problem money was invented to solve — and why the Central Bank of Nigeria guards the naira so closely.

blocks.markdown:
**Trade by barter** is the direct exchange of goods and services without money. It worked in very small communities, but it broke down as markets grew. The central obstacle is the **double coincidence of wants**: each party must want exactly what the other is offering, at the same time and in the right quantity. A fisherman who needs a cutlass cannot trade with a blacksmith who already has enough fish.

Barter also fails because many goods are **indivisible** (you cannot cut a live goat into change), **perishable** (they cannot store value), and have **no common measure** of worth. Deferred payments — wages, rents, debts — are almost impossible to write down when there is no unit of account.

blocks.title: Money
blocks.text: Anything that is generally acceptable as a medium of exchange, a measure of value, a store of value and a standard of deferred payment. In Nigeria that anything is the naira, issued solely by the Central Bank of Nigeria, together with bank deposits that can be spent by cheque, card or transfer.

items: **Commodity money** — cowries, salt, cattle, tobacco and manillas, each valued for its own use as well as for exchange.
**Metallic money** — gold, silver and copper coins, more durable and divisible than livestock.
**Paper money** — first as goldsmiths' receipts, later as notes convertible into metal, and finally as **fiat** notes whose value rests on law and public confidence.
**Token money** — modern coins whose face value exceeds the metal in them; they circulate because the law says they must be accepted.
**Deposit (bank) money** — current-account balances, the largest part of the money people actually spend.
**Electronic money** — cards, transfers and the eNaira, still claims on the banking system rather than a new species of money.

rows: Generally acceptable in payment for goods and services
Paying ₦2,000 for a bag of garri at the market
Prices and accounts are expressed in one unit
A teacher’s salary, a bag of cement and a barrel of crude are all quoted in naira
Purchasing power can be held over time
Saving naira in a bank rather than storing yams that rot
Debts, wages and contracts can be settled later in the same unit
A 90-day trade credit or a salary paid at month-end
blocks.caption: The four functions of money — examiners expect all four, not just 'medium of exchange'

blocks.markdown:
### Qualities of good money

For something to perform those functions well it must be **acceptable**, **portable**, **durable**, **divisible** into small units, **homogeneous** (every naira note of a given denomination is like every other), **relatively scarce**, and reasonably **stable in value**. Cognizability — easy recognition — matters too: that is why the CBN redesigns notes and why counterfeiting undermines money. Inflation attacks the store-of-value and deferred-payment functions even when the notes remain perfectly portable.

### Motives for holding money and the money supply

Keynes identified three motives for **liquidity preference** — the demand for money to hold:

- **Transactions motive** — cash for everyday purchases; it rises with income and with the frequency of spending.
- **Precautionary motive** — balances kept for emergencies: illness, a sudden school levy, a broken generator.
- **Speculative motive** — money held to take advantage of expected changes in asset prices or the exchange rate. It is **inversely related to the rate of interest**: when interest (or expected returns) is high, people prefer bonds and deposits; when it is low, they hoard money.

The **money supply** is the stock of money in the economy at a point in time. In the simple classification used at this level:

- **M1 (narrow money)** = currency in circulation outside banks + demand (current-account) deposits.
- **M2 (broad money)** = M1 + savings and time deposits.

The CBN influences both through monetary policy; commercial banks create the deposit component when they lend.

blocks.title: Classifying cash holdings and reading M1 and M2
blocks.prompt: A trader keeps ₦20,000 in the till for daily sales, ₦15,000 at home in case a child falls ill, and ₦40,000 in a current account while she waits to see whether the naira will weaken further. Currency in circulation is ₦200 billion, demand deposits ₦300 billion and savings deposits ₦400 billion. Identify each Keynesian motive and compute M1 and M2.

steps.text: The ₦20,000 in the till is held to complete ordinary purchases — the transactions motive.
The ₦15,000 for illness is a buffer against an uncertain need — the precautionary motive.
The ₦40,000 waiting on the exchange rate is held in the hope of a capital gain — the speculative motive.
M1 is currency plus demand deposits: ₦200 billion + ₦300 billion = ₦500 billion. Savings deposits are not in M1.
M2 adds savings and time deposits to M1: ₦500 billion + ₦400 billion = ₦900 billion.

blocks.answer: Transactions, precautionary and speculative motives respectively; M1 = ₦500 billion; M2 = ₦900 billion

blocks.title: Do not confuse the functions of money with the qualities of money
blocks.text: Functions answer 'what does money do?' — medium, measure, store, standard of deferred payment. Qualities answer 'what makes a good money?' — acceptability, portability, durability, divisibility, scarcity. Mixing the two lists is one of the commonest ways to lose marks in WAEC and NECO.

points: Barter fails mainly because of the double coincidence of wants, plus indivisibility, perishability and the lack of a unit of account.
Money evolved from commodities through metals and paper to token coins and bank deposits.
The four functions are medium of exchange, measure of value, store of value and standard of deferred payment.
Good money is acceptable, portable, durable, divisible, homogeneous, scarce and reasonably stable in value.
Keynes’s motives for holding money are transactions, precautionary and speculative; the speculative demand falls as interest rates rise.
M1 is currency plus demand deposits; M2 is M1 plus savings and time deposits.
